    AI Overview
    To redirect both standard output (stdout) and standard error (stderr) to a file in Bash, use the &> operator for a shortcut or > file.txt 2>&1 for maximum compatibility. 
    Overwriting a File
    This replaces the file's current contents: 
    • Modern Bash shortcut:
      bash
      command &> output.txt
      Use code with caution.
    • Traditional / POSIX-compliant method:
      bash
      command > output.txt 2>&1
      Use code with caution.
       
    Appending to a File
    This adds the new output to the end of the existing file without erasing it: 
    • Modern Bash shortcut:
      bash
      command &>> output.txt
      Use code with caution.
    • Traditional / POSIX-compliant method:
      bash
      command >> output.txt 2>&1
      Use code with caution.
       
    Redirecting to Separate Files
    If you want to view standard output and error messages in completely separate log files, split them using their file descriptor numbers (1 for stdout, 2 for stderr): 
    • Separate files (Overwrite):
      bash
      command > stdout.log 2> stderr.log
      Use code with caution.
    • Separate files (Append):
      bash
      command >> stdout.log 2>> stderr.log
      Use code with caution.
       
    Crucial Tip on Order
    When using the traditional method, the order of redirections matters. You must route stdout to the file first (> output.txt) and then direct stderr to stdout (2>&1). If you reverse it to command 2>&1 > output.txt, the errors will print to your screen instead of the file. 
    If you would like to expand on this, let me know if you need to: 
    • Silence the output entirely by sending it to a null device.
    • Print to the screen and save to a file at the same time using the tee utility.
    • Redirect output permanently for an entire script using exec.
